name: Linear Algebra: Vectors, Matrices, Tensor Products, Eigenvalues
short: The mathematical language of quantum mechanics: state vectors, linear operators, eigenvalues, and tensor products for combining systems.
detail: Quantum states are represented by vectors or rays in a complex Hilbert space, while observables and transformations are linear operators. Closed-system evolution is unitary; general physical processes can instead be quantum channels. Eigenvalues and projectors describe projective measurement, and tensor products combine systems into a 2^n-dimensional n-qubit space. Stabilizer codes are simultaneous eigenspaces of commuting Pauli operators. Logical Pauli operators are equivalence classes in the quotient group N(S)/S (up to phase), not state vectors in a quotient space. Bases, inner products, projections, and spectral decompositions recur throughout this tree.
key_points: Complex vector spaces, inner products, orthonormal bases, and the projection operators built from them
Hermitian operators have real eigenvalues and a spectral decomposition; unitary operators preserve the inner product
Tensor (Kronecker) products combine subsystems: n qubits need a 2^n-dimensional state space
Eigenvalues/eigenvectors: a state with a definite measurement outcome is an eigenvector of the observable
Matrix exponentiation and commuting operators: simultaneous eigenbases are the key to stabilizer codes
resources: Nielsen & Chuang, 'Quantum Computation and Quantum Information', Chapter 2
Gilbert Strang, 'Introduction to Linear Algebra'
3Blue1Brown 'Essence of Linear Algebra' video series (https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLZHQObOWTQDPD3MizzM2xVFitgF8hE_ab)

name: Complex Numbers & Dirac (Bra-Ket) Notation
short: Complex amplitudes are what quantum states are made of; Dirac notation is the compact standard notation every quantum paper uses.
detail: A quantum state is written as a ket |psi>, and its dual as a bra <psi|. For normalized pure states, a rank-one projective outcome |phi><phi| has Born probability |<phi|psi>|^2. Complex relative phases affect interference; a common global phase does not affect isolated-system predictions. Kets, column vectors, adjoints, normalized superpositions, and matrix elements such as <0|X|1> are standard notation throughout stabilizer and surface-code literature.
key_points: A complex number z = a + bi has a modulus and phase; |z|^2 is a probability only when z is the relevant normalized measurement amplitude
Ket |psi> is a column vector, bra <psi| is its conjugate transpose, <phi|psi> is the inner product
Outer products |psi><phi| are operators; projectors |0><0| extract components
Global phase is unphysical, but relative phase between amplitudes drives interference
The dagger (adjoint) operation turns bras into kets and reverses operator products
resources: Nielsen & Chuang, Sections 1.2 and 2.1
Andy Matuschak & Michael Nielsen, 'Quantum Country' essay 1
3Blue1Brown 'Complex Number Transformations & Euler Formula' (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mvmuCPvBiWQ)

name: Quantum Mechanics Basics: Superposition, Measurement, Entanglement
short: The physical rules of the game: superposition and interference, Born-rule measurement with conditional state update, open-system decoherence, and entanglement.
detail: Superposition means a qubit can be written alpha|0> + beta|1>, with relative phases affecting interference. A projective measurement samples eigenspace i with probability <psi|P_i|psi> and conditionally updates the state to its normalized projection; it need not disturb a state already in that eigenspace. Individual data-basis measurements generally reveal logical information and dephase an encoded superposition, whereas ideal stabilizer measurements reveal commuting joint parities. Environmental decoherence is an open-system process, not the same operation as a deliberate projective readout. Entanglement means a multi-qubit pure state cannot be factored into independent subsystem states.
key_points: Superposition: amplitudes add and interfere; probabilities are squared magnitudes (Born rule)
Projective measurement samples a Born-rule outcome and conditionally updates the state; environmental decoherence is a distinct open-system process
Unitary evolution is reversible and linear; the no-cloning theorem forbids copying unknown states
Entangled states like the Bell pair (|00>+|11>)/sqrt(2) cannot be written as a tensor product of single-qubit states
Complementary observables (X vs Z) cannot be simultaneously known — the root of quantum error correction's difficulty
resources: Nielsen & Chuang, Chapter 1 and 2
John Preskill, 'Physics 219: Quantum Computation' lecture notes (Caltech)
Andy Matuschak & Michael Nielsen, 'Quantum Country' essay 1-2

name: Qubits & Pauli Operators
short: The qubit is the unit of quantum information, and the Pauli matrices X, Y, Z — with their commutation rules — are the basic operators used to describe quantum errors and stabilizer codes.
detail: A pure single-qubit state can be visualized on the Bloch sphere. The Pauli operators X, Y, Z, and I form an orthogonal basis for single-qubit operators, so each Kraus or error operator can be expanded in that basis. If a code corrects a spanning set of Pauli errors on a stated support, linearity and the Knill-Laflamme conditions imply it corrects their coherent linear combinations. This does not mean every physical noise channel is literally a classical random Pauli mixture: coherent, correlated, leakage, and non-Markovian effects can remain. Pauli commutation and anticommutation nevertheless provide the binary algebra of stabilizer syndromes and logical strings.
key_points: Pauli matrices X, Z, Y = iXZ are Hermitian, unitary, and square to the identity
XZ = -ZX: Paulis on the same qubit either commute or anticommute — syndromes detect anticommutation
The n-qubit Pauli group (tensor products with phases +/-1, +/-i) closes under multiplication
Paulis span operator errors; correcting a Pauli basis for a stated support corrects its linear span, without turning every physical channel into a stochastic Pauli mixture
Bloch sphere: X and Z rotations, eigenstates |+>/|-> of X, and how Clifford gates permute Paulis
resources: Nielsen & Chuang, Sections 2.4, 4.2, 10.1
Daniel Gottesman, 'Stabilizer Codes and Quantum Error Correction', arXiv:quant-ph/9705052, Chapter 2

name: Quantum Gates & Circuits
short: Quantum computers run circuits of unitary gates; the Clifford group (H, S, CNOT) plus the T gate is the gate set whose fault-tolerant implementation is the main goal of TQEC.
detail: Quantum circuits arrange preparations, gates, measurements, and classical feed-forward along wires. Clifford gates map Paulis to Paulis under conjugation. The Gottesman-Knill theorem efficiently simulates stabilizer-state preparations, Clifford gates, and Pauli measurements; arbitrary non-stabilizer inputs are outside that guarantee. Which logical gates are transversal is code-dependent, and Eastin-Knill forbids a universal transversal set rather than every transversal non-Clifford gate. Surface-code schemes use a mixture of Pauli-frame tracking, code deformation, lattice surgery, and resource-state injection. A common logical T gadget consumes |A> = T|+>; its factory cost is algorithm-, target-, and architecture-dependent.
key_points: Core gates: H, S (phase), T, CNOT, CZ, and Pauli X/Z; universality needs a non-Clifford gate
Clifford gates conjugate Paulis to Paulis; the Clifford group is generated by H, S, CNOT
Gottesman-Knill: stabilizer preparations, Clifford gates, and Pauli measurements are classically simulable in polynomial time
Circuit identities: Hadamard swaps X and Z; CNOT propagates X forward and Z backward
Measurement-based gadgets (ancilla preparation, teleportation) turn gates into circuit primitives
resources: Nielsen & Chuang, Chapter 4
John Preskill, Ph219 lecture notes, Chapter 6
Qiskit Textbook, 'Quantum Circuits' chapters

name: Classical Error Correction & the Repetition Code
short: How redundancy protects classical bits: parity checks, Hamming distance, and the repetition code — the conceptual skeleton that surface-code X- and Z-checks inherit directly.
detail: Classical coding protects a bit by encoding it redundantly. The repetition code maps 0 -> 000 and 1 -> 111, and majority voting corrects a single flip. Several concepts transfer to quantum codes: distance, parity-check matrices, and syndrome-based inference rather than direct inspection of encoded data. A crucial twist is that qubit errors have X- and Z-type components. CSS codes—including the surface code—organize those components using two compatible classical-code structures; general quantum codes need not be CSS. In the repetition code, majority vote is the decoder; in a surface code, a graph decoder such as minimum-weight matching plays a related inference role under a declared noise model. Linear codes over GF(2), [n,k,d] notation, and noisy-graph inference provide useful foundations without making the two settings identical.
key_points: Repetition code: encode 1 bit in n, decode by majority; corrects floor((n-1)/2) flips
Hamming distance d determines error-correcting power; [n,k,d] notation for linear codes
Parity checks and syndromes: detect errors from violated checks without reading the data
Codes as graphs (Tanner graphs): checks and bits as nodes, decoding as inference
For independent low-p noise and a suitable decoder, the leading repetition-code failure probability has order p^ceil(d/2); correlations or a mismatched decoder can erase that benefit
resources: Nielsen & Chuang, Section 10.1
Arthur Pesah blog, 'Quantum Error Correction for Dummies' series

name: Stabilizer Formalism
short: The defining framework of quantum error correction: a code is the joint +1 eigenspace of commuting Pauli operators, and errors are diagnosed by which stabilizers they anticommute with.
detail: A stabilizer code on n qubits is specified by an abelian subgroup S of the Pauli group (not containing -I) with r independent generators; the codespace is the simultaneous +1 eigenspace and encodes k = n-r logical qubits. Pauli operators form an error basis: a Pauli component anticommutes with a generator exactly when it flips that generator's outcome, producing a syndrome pattern. General physical noise need not itself be a stochastic Pauli operator. Logical Pauli operations are equivalence classes in the quotient N(S)/S, up to overall Pauli phase, where N(S) is the Pauli normalizer. They can be represented by Paulis that commute with every stabilizer but are not stabilizers. The code distance is the minimum weight of a nontrivial logical representative. For CSS stabilizer codes, much of syndrome processing becomes linear algebra over GF(2).
key_points: Stabilizer group S: abelian subgroup of the n-qubit Pauli group; codespace = common +1 eigenspace
r independent stabilizer generators on n qubits encode k = n-r logical qubits
Syndrome of error E: the commutation pattern of E with each generator — no data is read directly
Normalizer N(S): Paulis commuting with S; logical Pauli classes form N(S)/S up to phase, with nontrivial representatives in N(S) \ S
Distance d = minimum weight of a nontrivial logical operator; degenerate errors act identically on the code
resources: Daniel Gottesman, 'Stabilizer Codes and Quantum Error Correction', arXiv:quant-ph/9705052
Nielsen & Chuang, Section 10.5
John Preskill, Ph219 lecture notes, Chapter 7

name: Quantum Error-Correcting Codes: Shor, Steane, CSS, Distance & Rate
short: The first quantum codes show how one logical qubit survives noise: Shor's 9-qubit code, the 7-qubit Steane code, and the CSS construction built from paired classical codes.
detail: Shor's code concatenates bit- and phase-flip repetition ideas to correct an arbitrary single-qubit error. This works because Pauli operators span single-qubit operators and the Knill-Laflamme conditions extend correctability from a basis of error operators to their linear span; it does not assert that hardware noise is literally a classical Pauli mixture. Steane's [[7,1,3]] code and the broader CSS construction (Calderbank-Shor-Steane) build X- and Z-type checks from compatible classical linear codes. Key parameters are [[n,k,d]]: physical qubits, logical qubits, and distance. The Knill-Laflamme conditions formalize when an error set is correctable, degeneracy allows distinct errors to act identically on the codespace, and coding bounds constrain achievable parameters. Surface codes are CSS codes with geometrically local checks.
key_points: Shor's 9-qubit code: concatenated repetition codes correct arbitrary single-qubit errors
Error-basis principle: if the Knill-Laflamme conditions hold for a Pauli error basis, they also hold for errors in its linear span
CSS construction: two classical codes give X-type and Z-type stabilizers that commute
[[n,k,d]] parameters; Steane [[7,1,3]] as the canonical small CSS code
Knill-Laflamme conditions and degeneracy: distinct errors may share a syndrome yet both be correctable
resources: Nielsen & Chuang, Sections 10.2-10.4
John Preskill, Ph219 lecture notes, Chapter 7
Daniel Gottesman, 'An Introduction to Quantum Error Correction and Fault-Tolerant Quantum Computation', arXiv:0904.2557

name: Fault Tolerance & Threshold Theorems
short: Fault tolerance constrains how faults propagate; threshold theorems show scalable suppression below a critical rate under stated locality, noise, and fault-tolerant-protocol assumptions.
detail: Every component of an error-correction circuit—gates, ancilla preparation, idling, and measurement—can be noisy. Naive syndrome extraction can therefore spread a fault into a damaging data error. A fault-tolerant gadget is designed so that the number and pattern of faults remain within the code-and-recovery guarantee; this is more general than requiring every single fault to become exactly one data-qubit error. Threshold theorems show that, under stated assumptions about locality, noise correlations, available operations, and the fault-tolerant construction, sufficiently low physical fault strength permits arbitrarily accurate computation with growing overhead. For particular surface-code circuits and stochastic circuit-level noise models, simulated thresholds are commonly around 0.5-1%; the number is not a universal hardware constant. A frequently used sub-threshold fit is p_L approximately A(p/p_th)^((d+1)/2), but its constants and even its useful range depend on the circuit, decoder, observable, and noise model.
key_points: Fault-tolerant gadgets keep fault propagation within a declared code-and-recovery guarantee
Fault-tolerant syndrome extraction: verified ancillas, repeated rounds, cat states, or flag qubits
Threshold theorem: below p_th, logical error can be suppressed with growing code size under the theorem's noise, locality, and gadget assumptions
Many specified circuit-level surface-code studies find thresholds around 0.5-1%; code-capacity and phenomenological models give different values
p_L ~ A(p/p_th)^((d+1)/2) is a common finite-size fit, not a universal law
resources: Daniel Gottesman, arXiv:0904.2557 (fault-tolerance sections)
John Preskill, Ph219 lecture notes, Chapter 8
Nielsen & Chuang, Sections 10.6

name: Topological Order & Anyons
short: Topological phases of matter store information nonlocally in degenerate ground states, and their quasiparticle excitations (anyons) have exotic braiding statistics — the physics that motivates topological quantum codes.
detail: In ideal models such as Kitaev's toric-code Hamiltonian, ground-state degeneracy depends on the topology of the closed surface and the ground states are locally indistinguishable. Under suitable conditions this structure is stable against sufficiently weak local perturbations, but a finite code is not immune to local noise and still requires active correction. The toric code has e and m excitations and their composite fermion ψ. Open string operators create excitations at their ends; taking e around m produces a -1 mutual-braiding phase. Contractible closed strings act as stabilizers in the ground space, while non-contractible cycles can act logically. This supplies intuition for surface-code syndromes, logical strings, and carefully scheduled code deformations that realize braiding operations.
key_points: Ideal topological order: topology-dependent degeneracy and local indistinguishability, stable to sufficiently weak local perturbations under stated conditions
Anyons: quasiparticles with statistics beyond bosons/fermions; e and m in the toric code braid to -1
Open strings create anyon pairs; contractible closed strings are stabilizers, while non-contractible cycles can implement logical operations
Fusion rules (e x e = 1, e x m = psi) govern how excitations combine and annihilate
In the ideal code space, sufficiently local observables cannot distinguish logical ground states; finite-distance protection is not immunity to noise
resources: Alexei Kitaev, 'Fault-tolerant quantum computation by anyons', arXiv:quant-ph/9707021
John Preskill, Ph219 lecture notes (chapter on topological quantum computation)
Fowler et al., 'Surface codes: Towards practical large-scale quantum computation', arXiv:1208.0928 (intro sections)

name: The Toric Code
short: Kitaev's foundational topological code: qubits on the edges of a torus lattice, star and plaquette stabilizers, and logical operators that wind around the torus's non-contractible loops.
detail: The toric code places qubits on edges of an LxL periodic square lattice. It has X-type star stabilizers at vertices and Z-type plaquette stabilizers on faces; in the standard ideal layout they are local, commuting, and weight 4. The code encodes two logical qubits and has distance L. An X-error string flips the plaquette checks at its endpoints, so a syndrome reveals endpoints rather than a unique error chain. A decoder chooses a correction in the same boundary class; failure occurs when error plus correction contains a non-contractible logical cycle. As a commuting-projector Hamiltonian, the ideal 2D toric code has a constant gap to creating anyons, but it also has a constant energy barrier: at nonzero temperature it is not a self-correcting memory. Long-lived storage therefore requires active syndrome extraction and decoding.
key_points: Qubits on lattice edges; star (X-type) and plaquette (Z-type) weight-4 commuting stabilizers
Encodes 2 logical qubits on a torus; logical Z/X = non-contractible loops on lattice/dual lattice
Syndromes are endpoints (anyons) of error strings — errors are seen only up to homology
A decoding failure occurs when error plus correction contains a non-contractible logical cycle; distance is L on the standard LxL torus
The Hamiltonian has a constant anyon-creation gap but no growing energy barrier in 2D, so passive finite-temperature self-correction does not follow
resources: Alexei Kitaev, arXiv:quant-ph/9707021
Sergey Bravyi & Alexei Kitaev, 'Quantum codes on a lattice with boundary', arXiv:quant-ph/9811052
Dennis, Kitaev, Landahl & Preskill, 'Topological quantum memory', arXiv:quant-ph/0110143

name: The Surface Code: Boundaries, Planar & Rotated Codes
short: The toric code adapted to a plane: complementary boundary types let a patch encode a logical qubit, and rotated layouts reduce the data-qubit footprint in a widely studied TQEC family.
detail: A planar surface code replaces periodic topology with boundaries. In one common convention, a single-logical-qubit patch has two rough and two smooth boundaries; logical Z and X are string classes connecting the corresponding complementary boundary pairs. Exact rough/smooth naming and drawn orientation vary, so operator supports should be stated explicitly. The standard rotated distance-d patch uses d^2 data qubits, compared with d^2+(d-1)^2 for the corresponding unrotated planar layout, while check weights depend on the boundary and circuit convention. Boundaries, holes, twists, and lattice-surgery seams are central tools, but universal computation also needs preparations, measurements, Pauli-frame tracking, and non-Clifford resources. Under perfect syndrome information, distance d corrects up to floor((d-1)/2) adversarial Pauli errors; with noisy extraction, effective protection is a property of the full space-time circuit and decoder.
key_points: Rough vs smooth boundaries terminate Z-type vs X-type logical strings respectively
Common unrotated and rotated planar layouts use d^2+(d-1)^2 and d^2 data qubits respectively; the latter is roughly half asymptotically
With perfect syndrome information, distance d corrects up to floor((d-1)/2) adversarial Pauli errors; circuit-level distance is a space-time property
Syndromes live on the dual/primal lattices as defect (anyons) at string endpoints
Code deformation and lattice surgery manipulate boundaries, while a universal stack also needs state preparation, measurement, tracking, and non-Clifford resources
resources: Sergey Bravyi & Alexei Kitaev, arXiv:quant-ph/9811052
Fowler et al., arXiv:1208.0928
Arthur Pesah blog, surface-code tutorial posts

name: Syndrome Extraction Circuits & Measurement Schedules
short: How a surface code is operated: ancillas measure X- and Z-type checks with ordered entangling circuits, and repeated noisy measurements create a space-time decoding problem.
detail: A standard Z-check circuit prepares an ancilla in |0>, applies CNOTs with neighboring data qubits as controls and the ancilla as target, then measures the ancilla in Z. A standard X-check circuit prepares |+>, uses the ancilla as CNOT control and data qubits as targets, then measures the ancilla in X. Equivalent circuits are possible, but control direction and basis must match the check. CNOT ordering matters because an ancilla fault can propagate into a hook error; a schedule is validated against the patch geometry so such hooks do not reduce the intended circuit distance. With noisy measurements, repeated rounds produce detection events defined as parity relations among measurement results and boundary references—not necessarily just adjacent-result XORs. A distance-d operation commonly uses order-d rounds around a boundary change, while a memory may run continuously. The resulting 2D+time detector graph is the input to space-time decoders such as MWPM.
key_points: Z check: prepare |0>, data-to-ancilla CNOTs, measure Z; X check: prepare |+>, ancilla-to-data CNOTs, measure X
CNOT ordering controls hook errors; schedules must be checked against logical-string orientation and circuit distance
Noisy extraction uses repeated rounds and a 3D space-time detector graph; distance-d operations commonly allocate order-d rounds
Detectors are deterministic parity relations among measurement results in the no-error circuit, often but not always adjacent-round differences
Circuit-level noise models include idle, gate, preparation, and measurement errors — this defines the real threshold
resources: Fowler et al., arXiv:1208.0928 (circuit and scheduling sections)
Google Quantum AI, 'Quantum error correction below the surface code threshold', arXiv:2408.13687
Higgott & Gidney, 'Stim: a fast stabilizer circuit simulator', arXiv:2103.02202 (detectors/space-time framing)

name: Decoding: Minimum-Weight Perfect Matching & the Threshold
short: A decoder maps check data to a correction class. For graphlike surface-code noise, minimum-weight perfect matching minimizes a declared weighted pairing objective.
detail: With perfect check measurements, nontrivial syndrome outcomes can be represented as defects on a 2D graph. With repeated noisy measurements, changes in appropriate parity relations become detection events on a 3D space-time graph. A decoder chooses a correction class consistent with those data; it cannot recover a unique physical fault history. For graphlike detector models, minimum-weight perfect matching (MWPM) pairs detection events or boundaries while minimizing the sum of specified edge weights, commonly derived from a noise model. That is an exact solution to the matching objective, but generally only a proxy for full maximum-likelihood decoding because degeneracy, correlations, leakage, and hypergraph faults matter. Threshold values must name their noise model: the standard toric/surface-code code-capacity value is about 10.3%, phenomenological models with faulty syndrome measurements are of order 3%, and common circuit-level depolarizing studies are around 0.5-1%. Experimental below-threshold claims are likewise scoped to a circuit, observable, decoder, and fitted distance range.
key_points: Decoding selects a correction class consistent with syndrome results or detection events; it does not identify a unique fault history
MWPM exactly minimizes its weighted pairing objective, which may only approximate the full noise-model likelihood
Space-time decoding: measurement errors become temporal edges in the 3D matching graph
Thresholds depend on model: ~10.3% code capacity, order 3% phenomenological, and commonly ~0.5-1% circuit level
MWPM approximates, not equals, maximum likelihood; degeneracy and correlated noise are its blind spots
resources: Dennis, Kitaev, Landahl & Preskill, arXiv:quant-ph/0110143
Fowler et al., arXiv:1208.0928 (decoding sections)
Arthur Pesah blog posts on surface-code decoding

name: Defects, Holes & Computation by Braiding
short: The original route to surface-code computation: punch holes (defects) in the lattice to create extra logical qubits, then braid them by slowly moving boundaries to perform logical gates.
detail: In a defect-based surface-code construction, holes or punctures create additional boundaries and logical string classes. A logical operation can be realized by a sequence of stabilizer changes that enlarges, shrinks, and moves defects so one winds around another. In an idealized topological description, homotopic distance-preserving deformations implement the same logical map. A physical schedule is not path- or timing-independent: geometry, separation, hook orientation, measurement rounds, and decoder boundaries determine circuit distance and overhead. Large defects and long schedules can make these constructions expensive in analyzed layouts, which motivated lattice-surgery alternatives. In specific foliated cluster-state constructions, the same logical history is represented by defect tubes in three-dimensional space-time.
key_points: A smooth/rough defect pair encodes one logical qubit; hole circumference sets the distance
Logical operators = loops around a defect or strings connecting defect pairs
A verified distance-preserving defect braid can implement logical CNOT; its ideal logical action is topological, while faults and overhead depend on the physical schedule
Defect movement = sequential enlargement/shrinkage with re-measurement, over many syndrome rounds
High space-time overhead of braiding motivated the shift to lattice surgery
resources: Fowler et al., arXiv:1208.0928
Raussendorf, Harrington & Goyal, 'Topological fault-tolerance in cluster state quantum computation', arXiv:quant-ph/0703143

name: Lattice Surgery: Merges, Splits & Logical Operations
short: Lattice surgery measures joint logical Paulis by temporarily coupling patch boundaries. In many planar layouts it offers a lower-cost alternative to defect braiding.
detail: Lattice surgery performs logical multi-qubit Pauli measurements by temporarily introducing boundary-spanning checks between surface-code patches. A merge changes the stabilizer group and repeated outcomes determine a joint logical parity; a later split restores separate patches but is not simply an information-free inverse. A standard logical CNOT uses an ancilla patch, two joint logical-parity measurements, a final ancilla measurement, and outcome-dependent Pauli-frame updates. Many Clifford operations can be compiled into Pauli-product measurements together with preparations, single-patch deformations or twists, measurements, and classical tracking; they are not all literally one merge/split pair. Planar patch layouts reduce footprint relative to particular defect-braiding layouts in many resource studies, but the advantage depends on connectivity, routing, distance, and workload. Space-time volume counts both occupied patches and code cycles.
key_points: Merge: measure joint stabilizers across a boundary for d rounds = logical ZZ or XX parity measurement
Split restores separate patch checks but does not undo the merge measurement; correlations and Pauli-frame information remain
A standard CNOT uses an ancilla, two joint logical-parity measurements, final ancilla readout, and Pauli-frame updates
Space-time volume (patches x code cycles) replaces gate count as the cost metric
Twists and boundary rotations enable Hadamard-like operations and patch reorientation
resources: Horsman, Fowler, Devitt & Van Meter, 'Surface code quantum computing by lattice surgery', arXiv:1111.4022
Daniel Litinski, 'A Game of Surface Codes', arXiv:1808.02892
Litinski, 'Magic State Distillation: Not as Costly as You Think', arXiv:1905.06903

name: Cluster States & Measurement-Based Quantum Computation
short: Measurement-based computation consumes an entangled graph state through single-qubit measurements; specific 3D cluster constructions realize a foliated topological error-correction scheme.
detail: In measurement-based quantum computation, a graph or cluster state is prepared by CZ-entangling |+> qubits, then consumed through single-qubit measurements. Universal computation generally needs adaptive measurement choices and non-Pauli measurement angles or equivalent injected magic resources; Pauli measurements alone remain in a stabilizer regime. Raussendorf, Harrington, and Goyal gave specific 3D cluster-state constructions whose correlation surfaces and defect tubes realize topological error correction closely related to a foliated 2D surface-code history. This is a construction-level correspondence, not a claim that every 3D cluster state is exactly a surface code. Their reported threshold is scoped to their circuit and stochastic noise model. The space-time picture motivates pipe diagrams used in some fault-tolerant compilation frameworks.
key_points: Cluster/graph states: |+> qubits CZ-entangled on a graph; universal resource for MBQC
Computation = adaptive single-qubit measurements; outcomes require feed-forward basis choices
Specific RHG 3D cluster constructions realize a foliated topological code; defect tubes encode scheduled logical deformations
Topological threshold in the RHG scheme ~0.6-0.75% under their noise model
Space-time pipe diagrams used by compilers are defect worldlines in this 3D picture
resources: Raussendorf & Briegel, 'A One-Way Quantum Computer', Phys. Rev. Lett. 86, 5188 (2001)
Raussendorf & Harrington, 'Fault-Tolerant Quantum Computation with High Threshold in Two Dimensions', arXiv:quant-ph/0610082
Raussendorf, Harrington & Goyal, arXiv:quant-ph/0703143

name: Magic States & Distillation
short: A surface-code Clifford toolkit is not universal; non-Clifford resource states can be injected and distilled, often at substantial architecture-dependent cost.
detail: Eastin-Knill rules out a universal set of transversal logical gates for a finite-dimensional code family under its assumptions; it does not say every useful logical gate must be transversal. Surface-code architectures commonly realize Clifford operations through tracking, deformation, surgery, or related gadgets, but have no transversal T gate. Using the convention |A> = T|+> = (|0> + e^{i*pi/4}|1>)/sqrt(2), a Clifford-and-measurement injection gadget can enact T. Toffoli or CCZ operations require corresponding resource states or synthesis from T gates, not the same single-|A> gadget. For independent input error p in the ideal Bravyi-Kitaev 15-to-1 protocol, the accepted output's leading marginal error is 35p^3 + O(p^4), with acceptance and correlations treated separately. Distillation factories dominated some early resource estimates, while later layouts reduced their cost in particular architectures. Factory importance remains algorithm-, hardware-, target-error-, and scheduling-dependent.
key_points: Eastin-Knill forbids a universal transversal gate set under its assumptions; surface-code architectures commonly use non-transversal methods for logical Cliffords and T resources
With |A> = T|+>, a Clifford-and-measurement injection gadget implements T; Toffoli/CCZ needs an appropriate resource or T synthesis
Ideal 15-to-1 Bravyi-Kitaev distillation has accepted marginal output error 35p^3 + O(p^4) for independent small input error p
Factories trade space x time for fidelity; space-time volume per T is the key cost metric
Later lattice-surgery studies found smaller factory overheads in analyzed architectures; no single fraction applies universally
resources: Bravyi & Kitaev, 'Universal quantum computation with ideal Clifford gates and noisy ancillas', arXiv:quant-ph/0403025
Daniel Litinski, 'Magic State Distillation: Not as Costly as You Think', arXiv:1905.06903
Gidney & Ekerå, 'How to factor 2048 bit RSA integers in 8 hours using 20 million noisy qubits', arXiv:1905.09749

name: Flag Fault-Tolerant Syndrome Extraction
short: Flag circuits add ancillas so dangerous fault propagation leaves extra information that a decoder or follow-up syndrome measurement can use under a stated fault model.
detail: A bare syndrome ancilla can propagate one circuit fault into a correlated data error. In a flag fault-tolerant construction, one or more extra ancillas and a carefully chosen gate order ensure that faults capable of producing dangerous data errors cause either a flag outcome or a syndrome pattern that distinguishes the allowed error set under the construction's stated fault model. A flag does not precisely identify every physical fault, and the guarantee is circuit-, code-, and decoder-specific. Such schemes can reduce ancilla overhead relative to verified cat-state or encoded-ancilla methods for selected checks and distances. Related flag-like checks also appear in small-code preparation and postselection protocols, including magic-state work.
key_points: Hook errors: a single ancilla fault can spread to a multi-qubit data error aligned with a logical operator
A validated flag circuit makes dangerous propagated errors produce a flag or a distinguishing syndrome under its stated fault model
Flag and syndrome outcomes narrow the allowed correlated-error set; they do not identify every microscopic fault
Ancilla savings and fault-tolerance guarantees depend on the code, check circuit, distance, and recovery procedure
Used in small-distance experiments and magic-state cultivation circuits
resources: Chao & Reichardt, 'Quantum Error Correction with Only Two Extra Qubits', arXiv:1705.05365
Chao & Reichardt, 'Fault-tolerant quantum computation with few qubits', arXiv:1705.02365

name: ZX-Calculus Basics
short: A graphical language where quantum processes are diagrams of Z- and X-spiders connected by wires, manipulated by rewrite rules — increasingly the front-end notation for lattice-surgery compilers.
detail: ZX-calculus represents qubit linear maps with Z-spiders, X-spiders, phases, wires, and Hadamards. Standard rewrite rules such as spider fusion and bialgebra are sound. Completeness is a theorem only for a specified fragment together with an appropriate complete axiom set: the stabilizer fragment has a compact complete presentation, while Clifford+T and universal qubit ZX require additional rules beyond the small introductory core. De Beaudrap and Horsman related lattice-surgery primitives to ZX diagrams, making ZX useful as an intermediate representation. Rewrites preserve denotation, but an optimizer's ability to reduce a chosen hardware cost is heuristic and compilation-flow dependent.
key_points: Two node types: Z-spiders (green) and X-spiders (red) with phases; Hadamard boxes swap colors
Core rules: spider fusion, copy, bialgebra, pi-copy, color change
Universality concerns representation; completeness requires a fragment-specific complete axiom set, not just the introductory rules
Lattice surgery correspondence: merges/splits = spider fusion/fission of measurement spiders
Serves as an intermediate representation for TQEC compilers and space-time volume reduction
resources: Coecke & Kissinger, 'Picturing Quantum Processes' (Cambridge University Press, 2017)
de Beaudrap & Horsman, 'The ZX calculus is a language for surface code lattice surgery', arXiv:1704.08670

name: Advanced Decoders: Correlated, Union-Find, Belief Propagation & Neural
short: Beyond vanilla MWPM: decoders that exploit X-Z correlations, handle degeneracy, run in near-linear time, or learn from data — an active race to close the gap between matching and optimal decoding.
detail: A basic CSS MWPM implementation often decodes X- and Z-type detector graphs separately, while real devices can exhibit Y correlations, leakage, crosstalk, and nonstationarity. Correlated matching can reweight or synthesize graph models that expose more of this structure; belief-propagation plus ordered-statistics decoding is another family, especially relevant to sparse parity-check codes. Union-find has almost-linear asymptotic complexity for specified topological-code decoding problems, but its threshold, accuracy, and wall-clock advantage depend on the noise model, graph construction, and implementation. Neural and tensor-network methods explore different accuracy/runtime tradeoffs. Google's Willow memory analysis used a matching-based decoder ensemble and synthesis, not belief propagation. Reported logical error and Lambda values therefore belong to the declared decoder pipeline as well as the device and circuit; there is no universally fastest or most accurate decoder.
key_points: MWPM ignores X-Z correlations (Y errors) and degeneracy; correlated matching/BP recovers much of the gap
Union-find has almost-linear complexity in its analyzed setting; accuracy and practical runtime are model- and implementation-dependent
Belief propagation + ordered statistics decoding (BP+OSD) handles degenerate and LDPC-style codes
Neural and tensor-network decoders occupy different accuracy/runtime regimes; neither is universally optimal
Willow used a matching-based decoder ensemble/synthesis; its reported Lambda is scoped to that circuit and decoding pipeline
resources: Delfosse & Nickerson, 'Almost-linear time decoding algorithm for topological codes', arXiv:1709.06218
Google Quantum AI, arXiv:2408.13687 (decoder ensemble methods)
Higgott et al., 'Sparse Blossom: correcting a million errors per core second with minimum-weight matching', arXiv:2303.15933

name: Real-Time Decoding & Classical Control
short: Logical computation stalls if the classical decoder can't keep up: real-time decoding demands microsecond-scale throughput, parallelism, and tight hardware integration with the qubit control stack.
detail: Every syndrome round (on a microsecond-scale cadence in some superconducting experiments) produces detector data. A streaming decoder needs sustained throughput at least as high as that arrival rate; otherwise its queue grows without bound, approximately linearly in time when the rate deficit is steady. Latency is a separate constraint: Pauli-frame bookkeeping can often be deferred, while lattice-surgery branches and magic-state feed-forward need decisions before their control deadlines. Solutions include parallel/windowed decoding (partitioning the 3D syndrome volume into overlapping windows processed concurrently) and FPGA/ASIC implementations. Hierarchical decoders handle most errors locally and escalate hard cases. Google's 2024 experiment demonstrated real-time decoding operating alongside the quantum processor, reporting 63 microsecond average decoder latency while sustaining a 1.1 microsecond cycle stream. The broader control problem — cryogenic wiring limits, latency budgets, decoder-quantum co-design — is now a central systems challenge on the road to large-scale systems. It sits at the intersection of computer architecture and quantum error correction.
key_points: Sustained aggregate throughput must meet the detector-round arrival rate; a steady deficit makes the queue grow approximately linearly
Throughput and latency are distinct: Google reported 63 microsecond average latency while sustaining a pipelined 1.1 microsecond cycle stream
Parallel/windowed decoding partitions space-time volume with overlap so multiple rounds can be processed concurrently
Pauli-frame tracking can often be deferred, but lattice-surgery and non-Clifford feed-forward decisions have control deadlines
Queue behavior, decision latency, and decoding accuracy are separate properties that must be measured for a declared architecture
resources: Barber et al., 'A real-time, scalable, fast and resource-efficient decoder for a quantum computer', arXiv:2209.08552
Google Quantum AI, arXiv:2408.13687 (real-time decoding demonstration)
Battistel et al., 'Real-time decoding for fault-tolerant quantum computing: progress, challenges and outlook', arXiv:2307.09096 (Nano Futures review)

name: Magic State Cultivation & Injection Advances
short: A postselected magic-state preparation proposal that injects into a small code, increases fault distance through checked growth, then escapes into a larger matchable encoding.
detail: In the original magic-state cultivation proposal, a rough T-type state is injected into a distance-3 triangular color code, initially with fault distance 1. Cross-checks, code growth, and stabilizer rounds increase the accepted state's fault distance while postselection discards detected faults. The final escape stage grafts or code-switches the state into a larger matchable surface-code-style encoding. Escape is not automatically fidelity-preserving: it adds circuit faults and can dominate rejection probability or cost, so the full pipeline must be simulated. Under the paper's uniform depolarizing circuit model and at selected intermediate target errors, simulations found roughly order-of-magnitude qubit-round savings relative to selected prior methods. That is evidence for the studied regimes, not a universal recurrence, fixed yield, or asymptotic advantage over distillation.
key_points: Cultivation injects into a distance-3 triangular color code, cross-checks and grows with postselection, then escapes into a larger matchable encoding
The injected state initially has fault distance 1; accepted checks and growth raise protection while retries consume resources
The escape circuit can add errors and dominate rejection or cost, so it must be included in end-to-end estimates
Hook injection (Gidney 2023): use hook errors as a feature to inject non-Pauli states
Published simulations show about order-of-magnitude qubit-round savings only for specified noise models, baselines, and target-error regimes
resources: Gidney, Shutty & Jones, 'Magic State Cultivation: growing T states as cheap as CNOT gates', arXiv:2409.17595
Craig Gidney, 'Cleaner magic states with hook injection', arXiv:2302.12292

name: TQEC Design Automation & Compilers
short: The emerging toolchain that turns abstract quantum algorithms into fault-tolerant surface-code layouts: logical compilation to lattice-surgery space-time diagrams, routing, volume optimization, and resource estimation.
detail: A fault-tolerant compiler stack can translate an algorithm into a logical gate set, synthesize Pauli rotations or product measurements, choose error-correction primitives, route patches, schedule measurements and feed-forward, provision non-Clifford resources, assign code distances, and estimate physical cost. One Litinski-style representation propagates many Clifford operations into a tracked frame and expresses the remaining work as Pauli-product measurements; the Cliffords are accounted for rather than physically erased in every architecture. ZX rewriting can simplify a diagram or reduce a declared cost for some inputs, but no generic rewrite sequence guarantees lower T-count or space-time volume. Research tools such as TopoLS explore particular lattice-surgery layout stages. Their output is a logical layout or schedule candidate—not a chip-ready pulse program—and still needs hardware mapping, timing, decoder integration, distance validation, and an error budget.
key_points: Compilation pipeline: algorithm -> Clifford+T -> Pauli rotations -> lattice-surgery schedule -> physical layout
One Litinski-style framework propagates many Cliffords into a tracked frame and represents remaining work with Pauli-product measurements
Space-time diagrams describe logical occupancy and measurement schedules; they are not automatically chip-executable controls
ZX rewrites preserve semantics and may reduce a chosen cost, but optimization gains are not guaranteed
Resource estimation couples patch layout, factory design, code distances, and decoding — a co-optimization problem
resources: Daniel Litinski, 'A Game of Surface Codes', arXiv:1808.02892
Gidney & Ekerå, arXiv:1905.09749 (resource estimation methodology)
de Beaudrap & Horsman, arXiv:1704.08670 (ZX to lattice surgery)

name: Classical Simulation of Quantum Error Correction: Clifford & Hybrid Methods
short: Validating decoders and codes requires simulating noisy quantum circuits at scale: stabilizer (tableau) methods handle Clifford circuits, while hybrid Clifford+statevector factorization pushes simulation into the magic-state regime.
detail: Gottesman-Knill methods efficiently simulate stabilizer-state preparations, Clifford evolution, and Pauli measurements. Tools such as Stim add detector and error-model annotations for high-throughput Monte Carlo studies of declared stabilizer circuits. General non-Clifford simulation is hard, but hybrid methods exploit stabilizer rank, quasiprobability, tensor structure, low non-Clifford count, or problem-specific factorization. Bravyi-Gosset algorithms have cost exponential in a non-Clifford resource measure related to the number and structure of T resources, with accuracy and task also affecting cost; 'only T-count matters' is too strong. A simulator validates the represented circuit, noise model, observable, and sampling procedure. It does not certify omitted hardware physics, and finite Monte Carlo data cannot prove an exact failure probability. Hardware experiments and independent analytic checks remain necessary.
key_points: Gottesman-Knill: stabilizer circuits simulate in polynomial time via tableau updates
Stim-style tooling: detector/error-model annotations enable fast Monte Carlo threshold studies
Bravyi-Gosset-style cost depends on the non-Clifford resource representation, task, structure, and target accuracy—not solely a universal T-count law
Hybrid methods can extend tractable regimes by exploiting stabilizer frames, factorization, tensor structure, or low non-Clifford content
Simulation validates a declared model and implementation; it does not certify omitted hardware behavior or an exact physical failure rate
resources: Aaronson & Gottesman, 'Improved simulation of stabilizer circuits', arXiv:quant-ph/0406196
Bravyi & Gosset, 'Improved classical simulation of quantum circuits dominated by Clifford gates', arXiv:1601.07601
Higgott & Gidney, 'Stim', arXiv:2103.02202

name: Below-Threshold Experiments & the Road to Factoring-Scale Machines
short: Hardware surface-code memories now show logical error decreasing across tested distances, with claims scoped to a circuit, decoder, observable, and fitted range.
detail: Google's 2022 experiment made the first larger-code comparison, finding a modest average improvement for a distance-5 surface-code memory over distance 3; two distances did not establish a full exponential trend. The 2024 Willow experiment tested distance-3, 5, and 7 memories and reported clear below-threshold memory scaling. Using Lambda = epsilon(d)/epsilon(d+2), it found Lambda = 2.14 +/- 0.02, so Lambda > 1 means suppression as distance increases by two. The distance-7 logical error per cycle was 0.143 +/- 0.003%. A separate lifetime comparison found a factor 2.4 +/- 0.3 beyond the best constituent physical qubit; that ratio is not Lambda. The experiment also demonstrated real-time decoding for a distance-5 memory. These are major memory and decoding results, not end-to-end demonstrations of a universal logical gate set or an algorithm. Required logical-operation counts and error budgets remain algorithm- and architecture-dependent.
key_points: Key metric Lambda: logical error suppression per +2 code-distance step; >1 means below threshold
Google 2024: d=3/5/7 memory scaling with Lambda = 2.14 +/- 0.02 and d=7 logical error 0.143 +/- 0.003% per cycle
The separate 2.4 +/- 0.3 result compares encoded lifetime with the best constituent qubit; it is not the suppression factor Lambda
Complementary platforms: neutral atoms and trapped ions show logical qubit transport and high-connectivity gates
Memory scaling does not by itself demonstrate universal fault-tolerant gates or an algorithm; targets depend on the workload and full error budget
resources: Google Quantum AI, 'Quantum error correction below the surface code threshold', arXiv:2408.13687
Google Quantum AI, 'Suppressing quantum errors by scaling a surface code logical qubit', arXiv:2207.06431
Bluvstein et al., 'Logical quantum processor based on reconfigurable atom arrays', arXiv:2312.03982

name: qLDPC & Bivariate Bicycle Codes
short: Quantum Low-Density Parity-Check codes generalize surface codes, offering better encoding rates. Bivariate Bicycle codes are a prominent recent family.
detail: While surface codes require physical qubits to scale quadratically with distance (yielding a vanishing rate k/n), qLDPC codes allow constant or higher rates by using non-local connectivity. The Tanner graph of a qLDPC code has bounded degree, meaning each qubit participates in a small number of checks. Bivariate Bicycle codes, a specific construction of qLDPC codes, have recently shown high performance and have been proposed for near-term implementation on architectures with suitable long-range connectivity, bridging the gap between hardware constraints and the asymptotic benefits of qLDPC.
key_points: qLDPC codes generalize surface codes with bounded-weight checks but non-local connectivity
They can achieve constant encoding rates (k/n) as distance increases
Tanner graphs visualize the connections between data qubits and parity checks
Bivariate Bicycle codes are a high-performance family of qLDPC codes recently proposed for hardware
resources: Bravyi et al., 'High-threshold and low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum memory', arXiv:2308.07915
